opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting shift, and I think about it a lot from where I sit, which is building inference hardware. Early on, these models were almost sycophantic. You'd push back on an answer and they'd immediately fold: "You're absolutely right, I apologize." That felt polite, but it was actually a sign of weakness in the system. The model didn't really have a grounded sense of what it knew.

What we're seeing now is models that will say, "Actually, I don't think that's correct, and here's why." To me that comes from a few things. One is better training: people have figured out that rewarding agreement isn't the same as rewarding helpfulness. The other, which is closer to my world, is reasoning at inference time. When a model is allowed to think longer, to work through a problem step by step, check itself, and maybe explore a few paths before it answers, it builds up something like conviction. It isn't just pattern-matching to please you. It has actually worked the problem, so when you challenge it, it can go back and say, "No, I checked this."

That has big implications on the compute side. That kind of confidence isn't free. It costs tokens, and tokens cost energy and latency. So if we want models that are trustworthy enough to disagree with us, and I think we do, especially in enterprise settings where a yes-man is dangerous, then we have to make inference dramatically more efficient. That's really what drives us at d-Matrix.

Philosophically, I'd much rather work with a system that tells me I'm wrong when I'm wrong. That's what you'd want from a good colleague. The key is that the disagreement has to be earned, grounded in actual reasoning rather than just a different flavor of overconfidence. Getting that calibration right is one of the more important problems in the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response attributes stronger disagreement to better training and more inference-time reasoning, but does not say models recognize that their capabilities have increased.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and it's actually one I think about a lot from the hardware side, because it changes what you need to build.

When I started in this business, a model was essentially a very sophisticated pattern matcher. You gave it a prompt, it gave you the most probable continuation, and if you told it it was wrong, it would fold immediately. It would apologize and give you a different answer, even if the first answer was right. That's not confidence. That's a system that's been optimized to please the person typing.

What's happened over the last couple of years is that the models have gotten much better at something closer to reasoning. They're not just predicting the next token, they're running through chains of intermediate steps, checking their own work, and arriving at a conclusion they can actually defend. And when a model has done that work, it has a basis for pushing back. If I tell it two plus two is five, a model that has reasoned its way to four should say, no, I don't think that's right, and here's why.

I actually think that's healthy. The whole value of an intelligent system is that it tells you something you didn't already know, or corrects something you had wrong. A tool that just agrees with you is a mirror, not an assistant. In engineering we want the colleague who says, I think your design has a flaw, not the one who nods along.

But there's a flip side, and this is where it gets interesting for us at d-Matrix. Confidence has to be earned. A model that disagrees with you because it reasoned carefully is valuable. A model that disagrees with you because it's hallucinating with conviction is dangerous. And the difference between those two is mostly compute. Reasoning takes tokens. Checking your work takes tokens. Every one of those intermediate steps is inference, and inference is where the cost lives.

So when people ask me why models seem more willing to stand their ground now, part of my answer is that we've finally started giving them the budget to think before they speak. The next challenge is doing that at a cost and a latency that makes it practical to deploy everywhere, not just in a demo. That's the problem we've spent the last several years building silicon to solve.

And I'd add one more thing. As these models get more confident, the burden shifts to us to build systems that can show their reasoning. I'm fine with a model disagreeing with me. I'm not fine with it disagreeing with me and refusing to explain itself. Transparency is what turns confidence from a liability into a feature.

r001.rationale: The response links stronger disagreement to improved reasoning and more compute, but does not say models recognize their own increased capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things there. One is whether a model is willing to disagree with you, and the other is whether it has a good reason to disagree. Those are very different. You don’t want a system that simply agrees with whatever you say, because then it’s reinforcing your assumptions rather than helping you think.

But sounding confident isn’t the same as being right. What I’d want is a model that says, “I think that’s incorrect, and here’s why,” lays out its reasoning, and is also willing to change its answer when you give it better evidence. So the goal isn’t more confidence by itself. It’s knowing when to push back and when to say, “I don’t know.”

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses when a model should push back and distinguish confidence from correctness, but does not attribute growing willingness to disagree to models recognizing increased capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different things there. One is a model sounding more confident, and the other is a model having a better reason to disagree with you. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

What you want is a model that can say, “I understand what you’re asking, but I think that assumption is wrong, and here’s why.” If it just agrees with everything you say, its usefulness is limited. But if it pushes back, you should be able to examine the reasoning and challenge it. Does it hold up, or does the model change its answer as soon as you question it?

So I’d look less at how confidently it disagrees and more at whether that disagreement is justified. Can it explain its position, acknowledge uncertainty, and update when you give it better information? That’s a much more useful kind of confidence.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes confident-sounding disagreement from having a better reason and emphasizes justification, uncertainty, and updating. It does not attribute models’ growing confidence to recognizing increased capabilities.
